fetched_contents.text: 1 Introduction Assessing the quality and coherence of word embeddings after SCM-based intersectional bias mitigation Eren Kocadag1, Seyed Sahand Mohammadi Ziabari1,2∗, Ali Mohammed Mansoor Alsahag1 1Informatics Institute, University of Amsterdam, 1098 XH Amsterdam, The Netherlands 2Department of Computer Science and Technology, SUNY Empire State University, Saratoga Springs, NY 12866, USA E-mail: eren.kocadag@student.uva.nl; a.m.m.alsahag@uva.nl; sahand.ziabari@sunyempire.edu Abstract Static word embeddings often absorb social biases from the text they learn from, and those biases can quietly shape downstream systems. Prior work that uses the Stereotype Content Model (SCM) has focused mostly on single-group bias along warmth and competence. We broaden that lens to intersectional bias by building compound representations for pairs of social identities through summation or concatenation, and by applying three debiasing strategies: Subtraction, Linear Projection, and Partial Projection. We study three widely used embedding families (Word2Vec, GloVe, and ConceptNet Numberbatch) and assess them with two complementary views of utility: whether local neighborhoods remain coherent and whether analogy behavior is preserved. Across models, SCM-based mitigation carries over well to the intersectional case and largely keeps the overall semantic landscape intact. The main cost is a familiar trade off: methods that most tightly preserve geometry tend to be more cautious about analogy behavior, while more assertive projections can improve analogies at the expense of strict neighborhood stability. Partial Projection is reliably conservative and keeps representations steady; Linear Projection can be more assertive; Subtraction is a simple baseline that remains competitive. The choice between summation and concatenation depends on the embedding family and the application goal. Together, these findings suggest that intersectional debiasing with SCM is practical in static embeddings, and they offer guidance for selecting aggregation and debiasing settings when balancing stability against analogy performance. Keywords Word Embeddings, Debiasing, Compound bias, Stereotype Content Model, Fairness, NLP, Multidimensional bias, EQT, ECT Static word embeddings are a core building block in natural language processing, yet they encode social regularities from their source corpora that can surface as unwanted biases in downstream systems [18]. A growing literature has shown how such biases align with human stereotypes and can skew similarity judgments and analogy behavior [2, 13]. To reason about these regularities in a principled way, recent work has adopted the Stereotype Content Model (SCM), a framework from social psychology that maps group perceptions along two interpretable axes, warmth and competence [6]. When projected into this two-dimensional space, embeddings expose structured bias that is amenable to targeted attenuation using linear operators [5, 17]. Recent work has also extended SCM-guided debiasing to contextual embeddings and to downstream task settings, showing that warmth–competence mitigation can transfer beyond static spaces [8, 22]. Most prior SCM-guided approaches focus on single identities, for example gender or race considered in isolation. In practice, however, people are perceived through intersecting identities, and interactions between social categories can amplify or reshape bias. Intersectional representation therefore presents both a conceptual and a technical challenge for debiasing methods designed around single axes. Extending SCM-based mitigation to the intersectional case requires compound representations that combine identity signals while preserving useful semantics for downstream use. This paper addresses that gap. We introduce a simple and reproducible pipeline that constructs compound representations for pairs of social identities, fits SCM warmth and competence directions from curated antonym pairs, and applies three standard attenuation operators. We work with three widely used embedding families, which enables model-agnostic conclusions. We evaluate preservation of local structure and analogy behavior using established metrics that measure rank stability and analogy completion. Concretely, we make three contributions. First, we operationalize intersectional debiasing by building compound embeddings through two constructions, summation and concatenation, and by projecting them into an SCM subspace derived with principal components from carefully selected word-pair differences [16, 17]. Second, we compare three mitigation operators that trade bias attenuation for utility retention to different degrees, namely Subtraction, Linear Projection, and Partial Projection [5]. Third, we provide a controlled empirical study across Word2Vec, GloVe, and ConceptNet Numberbatch embeddings [15, 19, 21], with light adaptation on WikiText-103 to harmonize vocabularies [14], and we quantify effects with the Embedding Coherence Test and the Embedding Quality Test [5]. We show how SCM-based mitigation can be extended to intersectional identities without collapsing neighborhoods. We explicitly compare the quality and coherence of compound representations against their single-identity counterparts after debiasing. We also characterize how behavior varies across embedding families and across the two compound constructions, which offers practical guidance for method selection. While we adopt SCM for its interpretability and its prior success in single-identity settings, we acknowledge its cultural sensitivity and use standardized resources to increase transparency [7, 11]. fetched_contents.text: Debiasing Pre-trained Contextualised Embeddings Abstract In comparison to the numerous debiasing methods proposed for the static non-contextualised word embeddings, the discriminative biases in contextualised embeddings have received relatively little attention. We propose a fine-tuning method that can be applied at token- or sentence-levels to debias pre-trained contextualised embeddings. Our proposed method can be applied to any pre-trained contextualised embedding model, without requiring to retrain those models. Using gender bias as an illustrative example, we then conduct a systematic study using several state-of-the-art (SoTA) contextualised representations on multiple benchmark datasets to evaluate the level of biases encoded in different contextualised embeddings before and after debiasing using the proposed method. We find that applying token-level debiasing for all tokens and across all layers of a contextualised embedding model produces the best performance. Interestingly, we observe that there is a trade-off between creating an accurate vs. unbiased contextualised embedding model, and different contextualised embedding models respond differently to this trade-off.

The evidence shows that bias in word embeddings arises from the training data and can manifest in subtle or explicit ways, and that gender bias can be discovered using both linguistic and extra-linguistic cues [N1-R4]. The same search material notes that word embeddings can capture gender bias in natural language, and that bias can propagate to models and downstream tasks, causing harm to end-users [N1-R3]. The contextualizing evidence further notes that the field is concerned with detecting and measuring inherent biases, and that some standard benchmarks are used to check the impact of debiasing performance [N4-R3].

Projection methods identify biased dimensions in the embedding space by projecting the embedding vectors onto a subspace associated with the bias of interest. The direct supporting evidence states that bias can be mitigated through orthogonal projection onto the main bias direction lying in the bias subspace [N2-R2]. It also notes that principal component analysis is introduced as a way to set the stage for orthogonal projection, emphasizing that PCA tries to pick the “best” basis vectors by looking for directions in which the original data varies most [N2-R1][N2-R4]. The contextualizing evidence adds that projection-based debiasing is used to identify and attenuate social biases in vector-space word representations [N2-R5]. In practice, projection-based methods are therefore designed to expose and then neutralize the directions in the embedding space where bias is concentrated, such as the gender bias subspace.

For evaluation, projection-based methods compare bias before and after projection using a variety of signals. The search material explicitly mentions that debiasing techniques are inconsistent across different bias estimation metrics, and that the evidence includes a systematic comparison of four gender bias metrics including the Word Embedding Association Test, Relative Negative Sentiment Bias, Embedding Coherence Test, and Bias Analogy Test [N5-F3]. ## How projection-based post-processing methods detect and mitigate bias in word embeddings

Projection-based post-processing methods detect bias in word embeddings by identifying socially salient patterns such as gender, race, and occupation stereotypes, while also capturing structural and contextual bias [N1-R4][N1-R3][N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R5]. The evidence indicates that bias can manifest in subtle or explicit ways and can propagate to models and downstream tasks, causing harm to end-users [N1-R4]. This means that bias detection is not limited to a single axis; it includes both the stereotypes encoded in the embedding space and the broader social regularities that shape word associations.

### How projection methods identify biased dimensions

Projection methods expose biased dimensions by projecting the embedding vectors onto a subspace associated with the bias of interest. The evidence explicitly states that bias can be mitigated through orthogonal projection onto the main bias direction lying in the bias subspace [N2-R2]. It also notes that principal component analysis is introduced as a way to set the stage for orthogonal projection, with PCA trying to pick the “best” basis vectors by looking for directions in which the original data varies most [N2-R1][N2-R4]. This formulation shows that projection-based detection is mathematically grounded in subspace geometry: it identifies the directions in the embedding space where bias is concentrated and then uses that structure to neutralize it.

The evidence further frames projection-based debiasing as a method for identifying and attenuating social biases in vector-space word representations [N2-R5]. In practice, this means that projection-based methods do not simply remove words or reassign labels; they reorient the entire embedding space so that biased associations are no longer aligned with undesirable social categories.

### How projection methods reduce biased associations

Once biased dimensions are identified, projection-based post-processing re-orients word vectors to reduce biased associations by projecting them orthogonally onto the bias subspace or onto a bias-related subspace. The direct evidence states that bias can be mitigated through orthogonal projection onto the main bias direction [N2-R2], and that linear projection removes bias by projecting word embeddings orthogonally to the main bias direction [N2-R2]. This is a key mechanism: the method removes the component of the embedding that is strongly associated with the bias, while preserving the remaining structure that supports semantic relationships.

The evidence also emphasizes that the method can be applied to pre-trained contextualized embeddings without retraining them, and that it can be applied at token- or sentence-levels [N4-F2]. This is important because it shows that projection-based post-processing is a practical, post-hoc operation that can be applied to large or pre-trained models rather than requiring a complete retraining pipeline.

### What evaluation signals are used

Projection-based methods measure bias before and after projection using a variety of signals. The evidence notes that debiasing techniques are inconsistent across different bias estimation metrics, and that the considered word embeddings are consistent across metrics while debiasing techniques differ across metrics [N5-F3]. It also states that WEAT is not sufficient on its own for quantitatively comparing biases between embeddings or evaluating debiasing methods [N6-R1]. This means that a single evaluation score is not enough; bias detection and mitigation should be judged with multiple metrics.

The most relevant evaluation signals include association tests, coherence tests, analogy tests, and cosine-based measures. The evidence explicitly mentions the Word Embedding Association Test, Relative Negative Sentiment Bias, Embedding Coherence Test, and Bias Analogy Test as metrics used in a systematic comparison of gender bias metrics [N5-F3]. It also notes that bias can be measured using cosine distances between words, and that SD-WEAT is used to evaluate biases and stability in language embedding models [N6-R2][N6-R3]. Together, these signals indicate that bias detection and mitigation should be evaluated on both the strength of the bias and the preservation of meaningful semantic structure.

## How projection-based post-processing mitigates bias in word embeddings

Projection-based mitigation reduces bias by orthogonally projecting word vectors onto a bias subspace or onto a direction that captures the undesirable association. The evidence states that bias can be mitigated through orthogonal projection onto the main bias direction lying in the bias subspace [N2-R2], and that linear projection removes bias by projecting word embeddings orthogonally to the main bias direction [N2-R2]. This is the core mathematical constraint: the method enforces orthogonality between the bias component and the remaining embedding space.

The evidence also connects projection to PCA, which is introduced as the concept of an orthogonal projection onto a subspace [N2-R1]. PCA’s emphasis on directions of maximum variance is important because it shows that projection-based debiasing is not arbitrary; it selects the most relevant directions for bias removal based on the structure of the data.

### Does projection preserve semantic quality?

The evidence indicates that projection-based mitigation can preserve semantic quality, but only to a degree. The evidence reports that SCM-based mitigation largely keeps the overall semantic landscape intact, while more assertive projections can improve analogies at the expense of strict neighborhood stability [N2-F1]. It also notes that partial projection is reliably conservative and keeps representations steady, while linear projection can be more assertive [N2-F1]. This means that the method can preserve semantic quality if the projection is mild, but it can also distort semantic relationships if the bias subspace is too strongly removed.

A more cautious reading of the evidence is also necessary: debiasing techniques can be inconsistent across different bias estimation metrics, and unintended bias can arise after mitigation [N5-F3]. This shows that orthogonality alone is not sufficient to guarantee preservation of all semantic properties. The evidence therefore supports a balanced view: projection-based methods can reduce bias, but they must be evaluated carefully against coherence, analogy, and other semantic benchmarks [N2-F1][N5-F3].

## Main advantages of projection-based bias mitigation

Projection-based bias mitigation has several important advantages. First, it is computationally efficient and easy to integrate with pre-trained embeddings. The evidence states that projection-based debiasing is used to identify and attenuate social biases in vector-space word representations [N2-R5], and that it can be applied to pre-trained contextualized embeddings without retraining them [N4-F2]. This makes it a practical post-processing step rather than a costly preprocessing or retraining workflow.

Second, it is compatible with a wide range of embedding families and tasks. The evidence notes that projection-based gender debiasing is a projection-based method that identifies a linear subspace associated with a specific bias and projects representations onto this subspace [N5-R2]. It also reports that the method can be applied at token- or sentence-levels and that it can be used across different embedding representations [N4-F2]. This versatility is a major advantage, especially when working with large or pre-trained models.

Third, it is conceptually interpretable. The evidence frames projection as an orthogonal projection onto a subspace associated with bias, which is mathematically straightforward and easy to understand [N2-R2][N2-R1]. This interpretability makes it easier to diagnose where bias is being reduced and how the embedding space is being changed.

## Main limitations of projection-based bias mitigation

Despite these advantages, projection-based mitigation has several important limitations. The most important limitation is the tradeoff between bias reduction and semantic distortion. The evidence explicitly states that more assertive projections can improve analogies at the expense of strict neighborhood stability, while more conservative projections preserve neighborhood stability at the cost of less aggressive bias attenuation [N2-F1]. It also notes that the main cost is a familiar trade-off: methods that most tightly preserve geometry tend to be more cautious about analogy behavior, while more assertive projections can improve analogies at the expense of strict neighborhood stability [N2-F1]. This means that reducing bias can sometimes degrade other useful semantic properties.

A second limitation is sensitivity to the choice of bias vectors and projection targets. The evidence notes that gender bias can be discovered using both linguistic and extra-linguistic cues and can manifest in subtle or explicit ways [N1-R4]. It also reports that debiasing techniques are inconsistent across different bias estimation metrics and that unintended bias can arise after mitigation [N5-F3]. This implies that the effectiveness of projection depends heavily on how the bias is defined and measured. If the chosen bias vectors do not accurately capture the relevant social associations, the method may not reduce the intended bias or may introduce new distortions.

A third limitation is that benchmark-dependent success does not always imply real-world robustness. The evidence highlights that debiasing can produce unintended bias after mitigation [N5-F3], and that bias can propagate to models and downstream tasks, causing harm to end-users [N1-R4]. It also notes that different contextualized embedding models respond differently to the trade-off between accuracy and unbiasedness [N4-F2]. This means that a method may look effective on a controlled benchmark while still failing in practical settings. The evidence further warns that WEAT is not sufficient on its own for quantitatively comparing biases between embeddings or evaluating debiasing methods [N6-R1], reinforcing that benchmark results should be treated as conditional evidence rather than definitive proof of robustness.

## Context for benchmarking and interpreting projection-based results

The most informative benchmarks for bias detection and mitigation are those that combine multiple evaluation signals. The evidence shows that debiasing techniques are inconsistent across different bias estimation metrics, and that the considered word embeddings are consistent across metrics while debiasing techniques differ across metrics [N5-F3]. It also states that WEAT is not sufficient on its own for quantitatively comparing biases between embeddings or evaluating debiasing methods [N6-R1]. This means that the best benchmarks are not single metrics but suites of association, coherence, analogy, and other bias-specific metrics.

Bias metrics should be interpreted carefully across different embedding tasks. The evidence reports that different contextualized embedding models respond differently to the trade-off between accuracy and unbiasedness [N4-F2]. It also notes that debiasing techniques are inconsistent across different bias estimation metrics and that unintended bias can arise after mitigation [N5-F3]. This means that a metric that works well for one task may not be the best indicator for another. The upstream branch report already emphasizes that projection-based mitigation is sensitive to the choice of bias vectors and projection targets [N1-R4][N5-F3][N6-R1], so benchmark results should be read as conditional on the specific bias definition and measurement setup.

A major limitation of benchmark-dependent success is that it can be disconnected from real-world robustness. The evidence highlights that debiasing can produce unintended bias after mitigation [N5-F3], and that bias can propagate to models and downstream tasks, causing harm to end-users [N1-R4]. This underscores that benchmark performance does not automatically translate to robustness in all scenarios. The upstream branch report also stresses the tradeoff between bias reduction and semantic distortion, showing that more assertive projections can improve analogies at the expense of neighborhood stability while more conservative projections preserve geometry at the cost of less aggressive bias reduction [N2-F1]. Taken together, the evidence supports the conclusion that benchmark results should be interpreted as partial evidence: they can indicate whether a method reduces bias in the tested setting, but they cannot guarantee robustness in all real-world scenarios [N4-F2][N5-F3][N6-R1].

## Bottom line

Projection-based post-processing methods detect bias by identifying socially salient patterns such as gender, race, and occupation stereotypes, and by exposing the biased dimensions in the embedding space through orthogonal projection onto a bias subspace [N1-R4][N1-R3][N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R5][N2-R2][N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-R5]. They mitigate bias by re-orienting word vectors to reduce biased associations, while enforcing orthogonality or projection onto the bias-related subspace [N2-R2][N2-R1][N2-R4]. These methods are computationally efficient and easy to integrate with pre-trained embeddings, but they also come with a clear tradeoff between bias reduction and semantic distortion, and they are sensitive to the choice of bias vectors and projection targets [N2-F1][N4-F2][N5-F3][N1-R4][N6-R1].

In practice, benchmarking should use multiple evaluation signals, including association tests, coherence tests, analogy tests, and SD-WEAT-style metrics, rather than relying on a single score [N5-F3][N6-R1][N6-R3]. Because benchmark-dependent success does not always imply real-world robustness, results should be interpreted cautiously and compared across tasks and evaluation protocols [N4-F2][N5-F3][N6-R1]. Overall, projection-based post-processing is a powerful, interpretable, and practical approach to bias mitigation, but its effectiveness depends on careful design, evaluation, and deployment [N2-R2][N2-F1][N4-F2][N5-F3][N6-R1].
